items.headline: September payrolls crater to +29,000 (vs ~89k consensus), unemployment hits 4.2% -- stocks rally hard, Fed-hold odds jump to ~83% for Oct 27-28
items.summary: The BLS reported just +29,000 nonfarm payrolls for September versus roughly 84-90k consensus, with unemployment rising to 4.2% (vs 4.1% forecast) and average hourly earnings up only +0.1% m/m (+3.0% y/y, the slowest wage growth since May 2021); August was revised down to +133k and July to -10,000, a net -60k two-month revision. Markets read it as bad-news-is-good-news for Fed policy: the S&P 500 rose 0.73% to 7,722.72, the Nasdaq gained 1.19% to 27,190.86, the Dow added 0.49% to 51,176.96 and the VIX fell 6.59% to 15.31, while fed-funds futures moved to price roughly 82.8% odds of a hold at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting.
items.actionable: This supersedes last night's preview and is the clearest signal yet that the Fed stays on hold rather than hikes or cuts this month, which is a mild net tailwind for the silver/miner sleeve and SGX banks' funding costs but not strong enough on its own to chase risk given the labor-market deterioration underneath the rally.

items.headline: 10-year Treasury yield hits a 24-year high above 5.3% on energy-driven inflation fear -- even the weak jobs print couldn't pull it down
items.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.34% intraday Thursday, its highest since April 2002, and held near 5.27-5.32% through Friday's close even after the soft payrolls report, as persistent Iran-war-driven oil inflation keeps the bond market pricing tighter policy risk than the labor data alone would suggest. The yield has climbed steadily from 3.96% in late February, the day before the US-Israel war with Iran began, underscoring that this cycle's inflation threat is coming from energy, not wages.
items.actionable: A 24-year-high real-yield backdrop persisting despite a weak jobs print is the key tension behind Friday's gold/silver pullback into the close and is a genuine headwind for the cash pile's opportunity cost calculus and for SGX REITs' refinancing costs, even as it's a tailwind for DBS/OCBC/UOB net interest margins.

items.headline: Tokyo core CPI runs hot at 2.7% y/y (vs 2.4% forecast, up from 1.8%) -- fastest pace in 10 months, firms up the case for another BOJ hike
items.summary: Tokyo's September core CPI (ex-fresh-food) rose 2.7% year-on-year, beating the 2.4% consensus and accelerating sharply from August's 1.8%, while core-core CPI (ex-food and energy) hit 3.0%, the fastest since August 2025; both exceeded the BOJ's 2% target by the widest margin since January. This actual print (superseding Friday morning's preview) vindicates the majority side of the BOJ's September 18 split 7-2 vote to hike to 1.25% and raises the stakes for the Bank's next meeting on October 29-30.
items.actionable: A hot Tokyo print strengthens the yen-carry-unwind risk that has periodically hit HK tech and SGX risk sentiment, so the October 29-30 BOJ meeting (just two days after the Fed) is now a second major regional-tightening catalyst to track alongside MAS's October 14 decision.

items.headline: Hang Seng plunges 2.7% to 23,943 (worst day since July) as Treasury yields spike and a new US ban on Chinese data-center gear hits tech; Stock Connect still dark until Oct 8
items.summary: Hong Kong's benchmark fell 667 points (-2.7%) to 23,943 on Friday as the 24-year-high US Treasury yield backdrop and a fresh report that Washington is moving to ban Chinese-made data-center components (optical transceivers, processors, networking gear) over security concerns hit sentiment hard; by Friday's close Tencent was down 2.27% on the day (-3.92% on the week) to 421.20, Xiaomi fell 3.96% (-8.80% wk) to 24.24, and SMIC dropped 0.66% (-5.56% wk) to 60.25. The selloff happened entirely without mainland participation, since Stock Connect remains suspended for Golden Week through October 7 and resumes only October 8.
items.actionable: This is a second distinct headwind for the HK tech sleeve layered on top of the yield shock -- a widening US tech/data-center decoupling campaign -- and it happened on thin, mainland-free liquidity, so expect an amplified reaction (either relief or further selling) once Stock Connect flow returns October 8.

items.headline: CityDev (C09.SI) craters ~14.8% for the week -- investors punish Kwek family's S$5bn China/Japan reinvestment plan announced alongside a S$6bn divestment drive
items.summary: City Developments unveiled a strategic review on September 28 pairing a targeted S$6 billion of divestments over three years with up to S$5 billion earmarked for new investments in markets including China and Japan -- a plan the market read as largely offsetting its own capital-recycling logic rather than returning capital to shareholders. The stock fell 8.1% that day to S$7.59 (from S$8.26 the prior Friday), then a further 2.1% on September 29 to S$7.43, and continued bleeding through the week to close Friday October 2 at S$7.04, a cumulative weekly decline of roughly 14.8% and the worst performer on the Straits Times Index.
items.actionable: This is a company-specific capital-allocation credibility problem (the market wanted net capital return, not a reinvestment pivot into China/Japan real estate) rather than a read on Singapore property broadly, so it argues against treating CityDev's drop as a signal to de-risk the SGX developer/REIT sleeve generally -- but it's a reminder to check whether other SGX developers announce similar reinvestment-heavy strategic reviews.

items.headline: Gold/silver spike on the jobs miss then fade into the close (GLD -0.72%d, SLV -0.02%d) as 24-year-high yields reassert themselves; miners outperform the metal again
items.summary: Spot gold briefly jumped above $4,190-4,210 and silver above $61 immediately after the weak payrolls print, but both gave back the move as the session wore on, with gold futures closing Friday at $4,172.10 (-0.72% on the day, -3.45% on the week) and silver at $60.71 (-0.02% d, -5.50% wk) -- consistent with the Treasury-yield backdrop staying elevated on energy-inflation fears even as hold-odds for the Fed firmed. Miners again decoupled from the metal: GDX rose 1.20% to 87.78 (still -5.48% on the week) and SILJ gained 0.44% to 27.23, both outperforming bullion's intraday fade.
items.actionable: The intraday pop-then-fade pattern confirms gold/silver are currently trading more off the real-yield/dollar axis than off Fed-cut hopes, so further payrolls-style misses won't sustainably lift the metals sleeve unless the 10-year yield itself breaks lower -- watch Treasury yields, not jobs data, as the next directional signal for the silver/miner positions.

items.headline: Bitcoin fades back to $84,511 (-0.40%d) after a brief push toward $87k; SEC proposes crypto-custody rule as BlackRock's IBIT snaps its inflow streak
items.summary: Bitcoin pushed toward the $87,000 area early Friday before fading to close around $84,511 (-0.40% on the day), tracking the same intraday-rally-then-fade pattern seen in gold as Treasury yields stayed elevated; crypto funds still pulled in a reported $3.55bn over the week even as BlackRock's IBIT ETF broke a nine-day inflow streak with $9.5m of outflows and Fidelity's FBTC saw $125.6m of withdrawals. Separately, the SEC proposed new custody rules that would let registered investment advisers and funds hold crypto assets -- including limited self-custody and state trust companies as qualified custodians -- with a 60-day public comment period once published in the Federal Register.
items.actionable: Bitcoin continuing to trade in lockstep with gold's yield-driven intraday pattern reinforces that it's offering no real diversification benefit to the portfolio right now, while the SEC custody proposal is a slow-moving structural positive worth tracking but not an near-term catalyst to add exposure ahead of the October 27-28 FOMC.

items.headline: Rare-earth basket: Lynas still down 8.93% on the week on Meteoric-deal dilution (China truce unaffected, extended to Jan 10 2027); USAR gets new CEO plus a Jefferies Buy
items.summary: Lynas Rare Earths (LYC.AX) bounced 2.45% Friday to A$12.95 but remains down 8.93% for the week, with the drop entirely attributable to dilution from its A$968m all-scrip acquisition of Meteoric Resources announced October 1, not any reversal of the China rare-earth export-control truce, which stays extended to January 10, 2027. Separately, USA Rare Earth completed its CEO transition to Thras Moraitis (from retiring Barbara Humpton) on October 1, alongside a fresh Jefferies initiation at Buy with a $21 target, even though USAR remains down roughly 36% over the past month.
items.actionable: Neither story changes the ex-China rare-earth thesis underpinning the basket -- Lynas's weakness is self-inflicted deal dilution and the China truce is intact through early January -- so this is a basket to hold through the noise rather than trim, while USAR's leadership change and Buy rating are a modest positive for the most speculative, most-drawn-down name in the watchlist.

items.headline: Oil diverges into the weekend (WTI -1.73%d to 91.26, Brent +0.38%d to 102.70) as Hormuz tail risk stays live: four vessels hit this week, Houthi missile intercepted, Trump vows war ends "after the election" with 9,000 more troops inbound
items.summary: WTI settled Friday at 91.26 (-1.73% on the day) while Brent held up better at 102.70 (+0.38%), a divergence against a backdrop where UKTMO reported at least four vessels struck by unknown projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz this week, a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at Saudi Arabia's Khamis Mushait was intercepted, and roughly 9,000 additional US troops are reportedly headed to the Middle East on top of the third carrier strike group already deployed. President Trump said over the weekend that he expects the Iran conflict to end 'right after the election, if not sooner,' offering no near-term de-escalation timeline.
items.actionable: The Hormuz/Houthi tail risk is clearly not resolving over the weekend and a sitting-president comment pointing to the midterm election as the war's earliest plausible end-date argues for keeping both the oil-linked inflation hedge and some gold/silver safe-haven exposure live into next week rather than fading the geopolitical premium.

items.headline: MAS tightening odds build into the October 14 policy meeting as core inflation hits a 2-year high of 2.2% -- a third straight hike now the base case
items.summary: Singapore's core inflation reached a two-year high of 2.2% in August, and CIMB Securities is forecasting MAS will tighten the S$NEER policy slope for a third consecutive meeting on October 14, after surprise moves in April (+50bps-equivalent) and July (+25bps). The Singapore dollar has held steady near 1.2780 against the US dollar through the week despite softer Asian FX broadly, consistent with the market already pricing in a steeper MAS stance.
items.actionable: A third consecutive MAS tightening on October 14 would extend the SGD-strength/bank-margin tailwind that has driven DBS/OCBC/UOB's outperformance versus S-REITs and developers like CityDev this year -- now the single most important SGX-specific date on the calendar, two weeks ahead of the Fed and BOJ decisions.

items.headline: PBOC bought gold at the fastest pace since 2023 in August (20.2 tonnes) -- a structural counterweight to dollar/yield-driven pullbacks, with Golden Week typically adding seasonal local demand
items.summary: The People's Bank of China added 20.2 tonnes of gold in August, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023 per World Gold Council data, extending a central-bank bid that has cushioned 2026 dips in bullion. China's Golden Week holiday (October 1-7) traditionally marks peak seasonal local gold-buying, though mainland trading itself remains dark via Stock Connect until October 8.
items.actionable: This slower-moving structural PBOC/seasonal bid remains the underlying support beneath the silver/miner sleeve even as this week's faster-moving Treasury-yield and jobs-data swings dominate the headlines -- a reason not to read Friday's gold pullback as a change in the longer-term demand picture.
